messages.subject: clear sky radiation vs real solar radiation
parts:
Hi Mike,
I calculated clear sky radiation and real solar radiation at lon=117.17, lat=38.87 in 2019 using micro_era5. However, I found the real solar radiation sometimes can be higher than the clear sky radiation (see the figure below, the blue line represents real solar radiation while the black line represents clear sky radiation). Could you let me know how this could happen? Your help would be most appreciated!

Best,

Liang

Hi Mike,

Thank you for the response! This is very interesting. Now I understand, that the "clearsky" parameter in the microclimate model only determines whether there is cloud cover or not, but has nothing to do with the aerosol condition.

If I want to get solar radiation data under a "true" clearsky, can I just set the "clearsky" parameter to 1, and in the meantime, set TAI to all zeros?

Best,

Liang

messages.author: 6cec8ea3702ece93
messages.subject: Re: clear sky radiation vs real solar radiation
parts:
Hi Liang,

You could set TAI to zero. But, if you really want to know what the radiation would be without the effects of the atmosphere, other than the permanent gases in the atmosphere that scatter radiation (a 'Rayleigh atmosphere') you could integrate the outputs from the drrlam table that are produced if you set 'lam = 1'. E.g. here's a plot of the Rayleigh vs the direct and scattered radiation at midday on the 15th Jan for the default location (Madison, Wisconsin):

library(NicheMapR)
micro <- micro_global(lamb = 1, IUV = 1, timeinterval = 12)
metout <- as.data.frame(micro$metout)
drlam <- as.data.frame(micro$drlam) # direct solar
drrlam <- as.data.frame(micro$drrlam) # Rayleigh solar
srlam <- as.data.frame(micro$srlam) # scattered solar
lambda <- as.numeric(colnames(drlam)[3:113]) # get the wavelengths
plot(lambda, drrlam[13, 3:113], type = 'l', col = 1, ylab = 'W/m2/nm', xlab = 'wave length, nm')
points(lambda, drlam[13, 3:113], type = 'l', col = 2)
points(lambda, srlam[13, 3:113], type = 'l', col = 3)

Black is the Rayleigh atmosphere, and then you can see the effect of water/aerosols/ozone in the red line.

Here's what you get if you just set the aerosols to zero (TAI = rep(0, 111)):



All the best,
Mike
